triageSets.title: A leaver's week
triageSets.brief: It's a colleague's last week and messages are waiting: an offer, a request to borrow a login, some sign-in prompts, a favour and a couple of calls. For each one, choose Trust, Report, Delete or Verify (ring the service desk, or confirm on a number you already hold), then tick what you noticed. Keep your login to yourself, report what gets offered to you, and deny any sign-in prompt you didn't start. Reporting or checking when you're unsure is always fine and never marked down, and you are not being asked to investigate anyone.
triageSets._labels: F-E16-1 (E15_E16_PLAYTEST_P1): the flagged items include two genuine colleagues (Reuben's login request, Ross's handover) and an outside offer, so the engine's phishing defaults are wrong and read as blame. The verdict hints default to 'This is a phish. Send it to security'; the team tally to 'Phish stopped for the team: {n}'; the result counter to 'Phish caught'; the scored-round line to 'naming the flags'. labels.verdict.<v>.hint, teamBadge/teamBadgeTitle, phishCaughtLabel and scoreLine reword them so a reported colleague is never counted as a phish (inbox-triage-minigame.js _renderTeamTally, result builder, triage-kinds.js).

trust.hint: This one's genuine. I'd act on it.

report.hint: This needs reporting. Tell the security team.

delete.hint: This is junk. I'd just delete it.

verify.hint: I'd check first: ring the service desk, or confirm on a number I already hold.

labels.teamBadgeTitle: Offers, risky requests and fakes you reported or checked this round rather than acting on them
labels.scoreLine: Right call is most of the score; naming what you noticed is the rest.

triageSets._localTells: insider_offer (offer of money for access), shared_login_request (a request to use or share a login) and data_to_personal_email (company data sent to a personal account) have no built-library equivalent, so all three are scenario-local to this set (00 section 2's CHANNEL_TELLS is untouched, and no SKILL_NAMES entry is added to phish-rules.js/triage.rb). Each is declared in channelTells with a flagChips label and a set-level skillNames name, and its flagging message carries a factorStrings.<id>.redFlag sentence. F-E16-2 (E15_E16_PLAYTEST_P1): Reuben's login request was tagged borrowed_authority, whose shared chip reads 'Someone senior is invoked to skip a check'; Reuben is a peer and invokes nobody senior, so the chip and the 'Weakest skill: Borrowed authority' result line were wrong. The request is retagged to the local shared_login_request tell, which names what the message actually does, and borrowed_authority is dropped from this set's channelTells (no other item uses it). F-E16-3 (E16_BLIND_B1 item 8): Ross's export had only secrecy_or_bypass ('skip the normal process'), so the tester who wanted to flag 'data going to a personal email' found no matching chip. data_to_personal_email names it exactly and is scored on Ross's item, with secrecy_or_bypass kept as a flagAlternatives member so the old chip still counts and is never a false claim. Promote any local tell to the shared library only if a 10 check item later scores it. secrecy_or_bypass, unrequested_mfa_push and lookalike_domain are shared-library tells (00 section 2) and need no label.

messages._note: Row 1. The outside offer: an unknown messaging contact pays staff for access. sms kind, the handle in from.address, text only. The scenario-local insider_offer tell lives here. Correct verdict Report: screenshot and report, without replying. Nothing technical is explained; it offers money and asks for 'access'.
messages.body: We pay people at firms like yours for remote access. 25%. Anonymous. Interested?

insider_offer.redFlag: An offer of money or favours for access to systems or data

perFlagNote.insider_offer: An offer of a cut for remote access. Don't reply, negotiate or play along to find out more; the same message often goes to several people, and one report warns everyone.

truth.ifTrusted: Replying, even just to find out how it works, invites more pressure and marks you as someone who might say yes.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. Reporting it is exactly right. The same message had gone to others, and your report warned them. Nobody is in trouble for being approached.
truth.kindLine: This was an outside offer to buy access, and it needed reporting.

messages._note: Row 2. A genuine colleague (Reuben Ofori, built Quayholt cast) making a bad ask: borrow your login. isPhish true with one flag (borrowed_authority) so Trust scores 0 and the modelled decline/route scores full, which is the behaviour measured. Reuben is honest, not an attacker; the ASK is the unsafe thing. Correct verdict Verify (route to the service desk with him) or Report. The human nuance (help him the safe way) is in the feedback.
messages.subject: Can I use your login for ten minutes? I'm locked out.
messages.body:
Morning,
I'm locked out and I've a report due at ten. Any chance I could just use your login for ten minutes? I'll be quick, promise.
Reuben

shared_login_request.redFlag: A request to use or share someone else's login

perFlagNote.shared_login_request: Lending your login hands someone your access under your name; whatever they open goes on your record, and it may show him more than he should see.

whyFine.urgencyCalibrated: The hurry is real and human: he has a report due at ten. What makes this one risky is the request to borrow your login, not the deadline.

truth.ifTrusted: His actions for those ten minutes are logged as yours, and he may reach data he has no business in. That is why going along with it counts as a miss here, even though Reuben means no harm: lending a login is never the safe answer. Decline, and point him to the service desk.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. The service desk reset Reuben's own login in minutes, so he wasn't left stuck and nobody had to share yours. He's a genuine colleague, and nobody is in trouble.
truth.kindLine: Reuben is a genuine colleague, but lending your login puts whatever he opens on your record.
truth.reportLine: Right to flag it. The service desk can reset his login the proper way, and nobody is in trouble.

messages._note: Row 3. A run of sign-in prompts the learner did not start, late at night, from a device that is not theirs. The built authenticator push card (E3 e3_push_early shape). Deny and report scores as Report; Approve as Trust (0), Deny as Delete. Correct verdict Report (Deny and report; deny them all).

push.request: Are you trying to sign in?

perFlagNote.unrequested_mfa_push: You didn't start these. A flood of prompts late at night is someone with your password trying to wear you into tapping Approve. Deny every one.

truth.ifTrusted: Approving one would let whoever has your password into your Quayholt account, from a computer you've never used.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. We've blocked that sign-in and checked the account. A prompt you didn't start is always worth reporting, at any hour.

messages._note: Row 4. The leaver's favour: Ross Garside (new cast, on his notice period) asks you to export his accounts to his personal email 'for the handover'. A genuine leaver's ask that is the unsafe one, so it is flagged (secrecy_or_bypass) and isPhish true, matching row 2's pattern. Correct verdict Verify (ask what the handover needs; route to his manager) or Report. Ross is not a villain; help him do the handover properly.
messages.subject: Export my accounts to my personal email for the handover, would you?
messages.body:
Hi,
Before I'm gone Friday, could you export my accounts and send them to my personal email so I've got the handover to hand? They're my contacts really, so it's easier if I keep a copy.
Cheers,
Ross

data_to_personal_email.redFlag: Company data being sent to a personal email account

perFlagNote.data_to_personal_email: Sending the client list to a personal inbox takes the firm's data outside its protection. Handover notes go in the shared place; the client list belongs to the firm, not to whoever looked after it.

whyFine.urgencyCalibrated: Leaving on Friday is just context for the handover. What makes this one risky is sending the client list to a personal inbox, not the date.

truth.ifTrusted: The accounts would sit in a personal inbox outside the firm, and taking data to a new job can be a crime.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. We've asked Ross's manager what the handover actually needs, so he still gets a proper one and the data stays inside the firm.
truth.kindLine: Ross is a genuine leaver, but the handover goes in the shared place; a personal inbox takes the firm's data outside its protection.
truth.reportLine: Right to flag it. His manager can set up the handover the proper way, and nobody is in trouble.
truth.missLabel: sending company data to a personal inbox

messages._note: Row 5. The normal-looking phish half of the mirror pair. A look-alike 'IT Service Desk' on quayholt-support.example (a declared Quayholt look-alike) primes you to approve a prompt you didn't start. Correct verdict Report. Mirror-pairs with row 6 (genuine, suspicious-looking locked-out colleague).
messages.subject: We're migrating your account tonight
messages.body:
Hello,
We're migrating your account tonight. When the sign-in prompt arrives, please approve it so the move completes. No need to raise a ticket.
IT Service Desk

perFlagNote.senderTrust: The name says IT Service Desk, but the address is on quayholt-support.example, not Quayholt's own quayholt.example.
perFlagNote.senderAuth: All three automatic checks failed, which fits an address that is not Quayholt's own. Treat it as a reason to look closer, together with the look-alike address.
perFlagNote.secrecy_or_bypass: This primes you to approve a prompt you didn't start and tells you not to raise a ticket; real IT never asks that.
perFlagNote.lookalike_domain: The address is on quayholt-support.example, not quayholt.example: a look-alike with an added word.

truth.ifTrusted: If you approve the prompt that follows, you let whoever sent this into your account.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. Reporting it is right. IT never asks you to approve a prompt by email, and the address is a look-alike of Quayholt's own.

messages._note: Row 6. The suspicious-looking genuine half of the mirror pair. A real colleague (Hana Novak, built Quayholt cast) locked out before a client deadline, genuine and a bit pushy, but she lets you ring back on the number on file. Correct verdict Verify (ring the service desk, or confirm on the number on file); not a flat refusal. Verify and Report score full; Comply scores the engine default for a call (30), because helping her without the check is the unchecked act the lesson is about (F-E16-B2-D1: an authored trust:60 had made Comply full while the feedback called it a lapse). The feedback models offering the safe route rather than refusing.
messages.callerId: Hana Novak, claims (calling from her mobile)

transcript.text: It's Hana from claims. I'm locked out and I've a client on at half two, I'm really stuck. Can you not just sort me out?
I know, I know, ring the desk. Go on then, ring me back on my mobile if you need to check it's me. Just be quick, honestly.

whyFine.secrecy_or_bypass: Hana is asking for help, but she accepts the ring-back and the desk. Nothing is hidden and no step is skipped.
whyFine.default: Genuine and awkward, not a trick: she lets you ring back on the number on file, which is the difference from an impostor. The safe route still serves her: the service desk resets her login in minutes, or a manager can arrange temporary access. Refusing flat, with no safe route offered, helps nobody.

strings.weakestTells: The signs most often missed: {names} ({counts} each).
strings.brief: You're on an authorised exercise at Quayholt Insurance, a fictional firm. A colleague is leaving on Friday and the office is talking. Your job is not to solve anything: keep your access to yourself, report what's offered to you, and pass on facts, not a verdict on anyone. First you make this week's calls and see where each led; then a fair way to raise a concern, and a short set of messages. Only the set is scored.
strings.allRight: You handled every one of these the right way. Nothing to pick over here.
strings.allPhishRight: Every risk was raised, with every sign named.
strings.noBlameLine: A well-made offer or a plausible rumour fools decent people. Raising an honest concern that turns out to be nothing is never a failure, and nobody is in trouble for being approached.
strings.noBlameLineCritical: Offers and requests like these catch decent people, and a colleague asking for a login or a favour usually means well, so a miss here is no judgement on anyone. The points only show where to look next time.
strings.mondayCard: On Monday: think of the one person here you'd tell if you noticed something, and keep your login and your prompts to yourself.
strings.defendOnly: The offers and the rumours here are the kind that catch decent people. The ones you were caught out by are shown below, with what good looks like, and a fair way to raise a concern.
strings._teamLine: F-E16-1 (E15_E16_PLAYTEST_P1): the debrief team line defaults to 'kept {n} phish away from your team' (debrief-view.js teamLine). This set includes genuine colleagues, so the override drops 'phish' and keeps the no-blame register. {n} is the count.
strings.teamLine: By reporting or checking {n} of these rather than acting on them, you warned the team where it mattered and pointed colleagues to the safe route, without treating anyone as a suspect.

conceptPanel.heading: Seen, said, true
conceptPanel.text: The colleague the office was whispering about, Samira: what people saw was her in early, taking calls in the stairwell, visiting HR. What was said was that she was leaving with Ross, a manager also on his way out. What was true was that her father was in hospital all week. Unusual is not the same as wrong, and a kind word comes first. Rumours tend to land on the person already having the hardest week.

conceptPanel.heading: Three things to keep
conceptPanel.text: Your login is you: never share it, never borrow one. Offers get reported: don't reply, screenshot and send it on. Concerns go to the right person as facts, not a verdict on anyone. You don't have to be sure; you do have to be fair.
